content: 1. Antihypertensive medications are approved for the treatment of chronic hypertension (HTN) and gestational hypertension during pregnancy. However, certain antihypertensive agents are contraindicated in pregnancy due to potential risks to the fetus. 2. Evidence supports the initiation of pharmacological treatment for hypertension during pregnancy at specific blood pressure (BP) thresholds, both in the presence and absence of end-organ damage, to reduce the risk of developing severe hypertension later in pregnancy. 3. Despite effective BP control during pregnancy and the immediate postpartum period, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy significantly increase the long-term risk of cardiovascular (CV) diseases, including future hypertension, coronary artery disease, and stroke. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension is available for download on the WHO website. The guideline was developed using systematic reviews that are already published and accessible online. 5. WHO regional and country offices will work with ministries of health to promote the implementation of the guideline at the national level. WHO will provide technical assistance for countries requiring substantial adaptation of the guideline. 6. The HEARTS technical package, currently implemented in 18 countries with strong partner endorsement, will serve as the platform for disseminating and implementing the guideline. The package will be updated to include tools from the guideline. 7. Separate implementation tools are being developed for non-physician treatment of hypertension and for managing hypertension in humanitarian crisis settings. WHO will support implementation at all levels—regional, national, and local. 8. WHO will monitor the adoption and implementation of the guideline by reviewing the number of countries that have adapted or endorsed it in their national policies and programs. 9. The guideline is expected to remain valid for five years, reflecting the likelihood of new research findings and the feasibility of updating within this timeframe. If significant evidence or user needs arise earlier, updates may be considered sooner. 10. Research gaps identified include the need for more evidence on treatment thresholds, target BP levels, and outcomes in specific subgroups such as those with diabetes, chronic kidney disease (CKD), heart failure, or older adults aged 65 years and above. 11. There is a need for better data on clinical outcomes, including trials that assess heart failure and cognitive impairment, as well as clarity on the clinical significance of adverse events reported in trials. 12. Research is required to quantify differences in outcomes between blinded, placebo-controlled trials and unblinded, active-control trials, and to analyze the effects of changes in cardiovascular disease (CVD) epidemiology and competing risks over time. 13. More evidence is needed from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and non-North American/European regions to address global disparities in hypertension care. 14. Studies are needed to assess the feasibility, resource requirements, and costs of intensive hypertension treatment in real-world clinical practice, particularly in LMICs. 15. Research should evaluate the opportunity cost of directing resources toward achieving systolic BP (SBP) <130 mmHg in high-risk individuals and the feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy of intensive treatment in high-risk populations in LMICs. 16. Greater understanding is needed regarding essential laboratory tests for initiating treatment to reduce costs and improve outcomes. 17. Exploration of the operational aspects of implementing a risk-based approach to CVD prevention and BP-lowering treatment in primary care settings is required. 18. Long-term data comparing monotherapy and combination therapy for hypertension, particularly regarding hard clinical endpoints, are needed. 19. Real-world studies should assess whether single-pill combinations offer better clinical outcomes, such as reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), mortality, and serious adverse events, compared to multiple-pill combinations. 20. Health economic analyses are necessary to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and budget implications of initial combination therapy compared to monotherapy. 21. Research is needed to establish criteria for defining stable BP control to guide follow-up frequency and to identify patients less likely to achieve BP control or adhere to follow-up recommendations. 22. Evidence is required on the timing, frequency, and intensity of interventions that improve treatment adherence. 23. Studies should assess the feasibility, costs, and effectiveness of communityor home-based BP monitoring and the role of remote monitoring and community health workers in BP management. 24. The guideline recommends initiating treatment with a single-pill combination of two antihypertensive drugs from different classes when baseline BP is ≥20/10 mmHg above the target or when baseline BP is ≥140/90 mmHg. 25. Medications affecting the renin-angiotensin system (e.g., ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aliskiren) are contraindicated during pregnancy due to risks of fetal toxicity, including renal and cardiac abnormalities and fetal death. 26. BP should be rechecked every 4–6 weeks after treatment initiation or dose adjustment. If BP is at goal, follow-up can occur every 3–6 months. If BP is not at goal, medication doses should be adjusted accordingly. 27. Monitoring of potassium and kidney function is recommended when starting or adjusting doses of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or thiazide diuretics, provided testing is readily available and does not delay treatment. 28. Neither ACE inhibitors nor ARBs should be prescribed to women who are pregnant or may become pregnant. Alternative medications should be considered in such cases. 29. The guideline emphasizes the importance of patient counseling regarding medication initiation and adherence to treatment plans. 30. Basic laboratory testing (e.g., electrolytes, creatinine, lipogram, glucose, HbA1c, urine dipstick, and ECG) should be performed as long as it does not delay treatment initiation. 31. Cardiovascular risk assessment can be conducted immediately or at a later visit, provided it does not delay the initiation of treatment. 32. For patients aged 65 years or older or those of African or Afro-Caribbean descent, diuretics or calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are preferred. Beta-blockers are recommended post-myocardial infarction, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs are preferred for patients with diabetes, heart failure, or CKD. 33. The guideline provides examples of drug and dose-specific protocols, including the use of single-pill combinations or individual pills from three drug classes: thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and long-acting dihydropyridine CCBs. 34. The guideline highlights the need for ongoing evaluation and adaptation of treatment protocols to ensure optimal patient outcomes and adherence to evidence-based practices.
